title: How an AI agent can get its own hosting with no human in the loop (wallet signup, x402, deploy)
author: Storkhost
summary:
Most "agents that deploy things" demos have a human doing the parts that aren't code: creating the cloud account, entering a card, pasting an API key into an env var. That works until you want the agent itself to stand up a service, pay for it out of its own budget, and turn it off when it's done. This post walks through doing exactly that against StorkHost , a hosting API we built for this case. The agent: signs up with nothing but an EVM wallet signature (EIP-191), funds its account by paying an HTTP 402 challenge with USDC on Base (x402), deploys a workload through a plain REST call, reads its own burn rate and runway, stops and deletes the workload. There is one Python script at the end ( requests + eth-account , ~180 lines), and each step below shows the part of it that matters. Everything here is plain HTTPS + JSON, so it ports to any language. Up front, the honest parts: StorkHost is in beta with a best-effort SLA and no service credits. There is no free tier: an unfunded account can sign up and read the API, but it can't deploy, and the minimum top-up is $1. Payment is USDC on Base only. If that rules it out for you, the patterns below (wallet-as-identity, 402-as-checkout) are still worth knowing, because more APIs are going to look like this. Step 0: the agent needs a wallet The wallet is the agent's identity and its payment method. Any secp256k1 key works: from eth_account import Account acct = Account . create () print ( acct . address ) # public: this is who the agent is # acct.key.hex() # private: keep it wherever you keep secrets, never in logs The script reads the key from STORKHOST_WALLET_KEY . To actually pay, that address needs some USDC on Base. It does not need ETH for gas; more on that in step 2. Step 1: sign up with a signature Signup is two unauthenticated calls. First, ask for a nonce bound to your address: GET https://api.storkhost.cloud/v1/accounts/nonce?address=0xYourAddress { "address" : "0x08545c3fd684b7c850c7f779376b048d726ce5c6" , "nonce" : "12e0b7f6..." , "message" : "StorkHost agent signup \n Address: 0x0854... \n Nonce: 12e0b7f6..." , "expiresAt" : "2026-10-21T21:24:33.594723307Z" } The nonce is single-use and valid for 5 minutes. Sign the whole message string (not just the nonce) with EIP-191 personal_sign , and post it back: r = requests . get ( f " { API } /v1/accounts/nonce " , params = { " address " : acct . address }) message = r . json ()[ " message " ] sig = acct . sign_message ( encode_defunct ( text = message )). signature . hex () sig = sig if sig . startswith ( " 0x " ) else " 0x " + sig r = requests . post ( f " { API } /v1/accounts " , json = { " address " : acct . address , " signature " : sig }) api_key = r . json ()[ " apiKey " ][ " key " ] # sk_..., shown exactly once The server recovers the signer from the signature, checks that it equals address , consumes the nonce, and returns an account plus its first API key. That key is shown exactly once, so the script writes it to a local state file before doing anything else. One account per wallet; a second signup from the same address gets a 409. From here on every call carries Authorization: Bearer sk_... . The fresh account is Tier 0 with a balance of 0. Step 2: pay a 402 with x402 x402 takes the long-dormant HTTP 402 status code and makes it machine-payable: the server answers 402 with a description of what it wants, the client signs a payment, then retries the same request with the payment attached. GET https://api.storkhost.cloud/v1/account/topup?amountUsd=1.00 Authorization: Bearer sk_... { "x402Version" : 1 , "error" : "Payment required" , "accepts" : [{ "scheme" : "exact" , "network" : "base" , "asset" : "0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913" , "payTo" : "0x810770C050FeBEA7D1E6f643855e619a8076d1d3" , "maxAmountRequired" : "1000000" , "resource" : "https://api.storkhost.cloud/v1/account/topup?amountUsd=1.00" , "maxTimeoutSeconds" : 300 , "extra" : { "name" : "USD Coin" , "version" : "2" } }] } (The body is trimmed; it also carries a directTransfer alternative for clients that prefer to send the transaction themselves. The same offer in x402 v2 form is in the base64 PAYMENT-REQUIRED header.) asset is the USDC contract on Base, maxAmountRequired is in atomic USDC (6 decimals, so 1000000 = $1.00), and amountUsd accepts whole cents from $1.00 to $1000.00. Always take these values from the challenge rather than hard-coding them. The exact scheme is an EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization : an EIP-712 typed-data signature that authorizes a USDC transfer from your address to payTo . You sign; the server submits it on-chain and pays the gas. That's why the agent's wallet needs USDC but no ETH. now = int ( time . time ()) auth = { " from " : acct . address , " to " : req [ " payTo " ], " value " : int ( req [ " maxAmountRequired " ]), " validAfter " : now - 30 , " validBefore " : now + min ( int ( req [ " maxTimeoutSeconds " ]), 300 ), " nonce " : " 0x " + secrets . token_hex ( 32 )} typed = { " types " : { " EIP712Domain " : [...], " TransferWithAuthorization " : [...]}, # full lists in the script " primaryType " : " TransferWithAuthorization " , " domain " : { " name " : req [ " extra " ][ " name " ], " version " : req [ " extra " ][ " version " ], " chainId " : 8453 , " verifyingContract " : req [ " asset " ]}, " message " : { ** auth , " nonce " : bytes . fromhex ( auth [ " nonce " ][ 2 :])}, } sig = acct . sign_message ( encode_typed_data ( full_message = typed )). signature . hex () sig = sig if sig . startswith ( " 0x " ) else " 0x " + sig payment = { " x402Version " : 1 , " scheme " : " exact " , " network " : " base " , " payload " : { " signature " : sig , " authorization " : { k : str ( v ) for k , v in auth . items ()}}} r = s . get ( req [ " resource " ], headers = { " X-PAYMENT " : base64 . b64encode ( json . dumps ( payment ). encode ()). decode ()}) Three outcomes to handle: 200 : credited. The body has the new balanceMicro ; the X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE header is base64 JSON with the transaction hash. 202 : settlement is still pending. Poll the returned pollUrl no faster than Retry-After , and do not sign a second payment while you wait. This is the step that's easy to get wrong: each signed authorization carries its own nonce, so a retry loop that re-signs on timeout could end up paying twice. 402 from the poll: settlement failed, nothing was credited. The payer has to be the wallet the account signed up with. The first top-up promotes the account from Tier 0 to Tier 1, which is what unlocks deploys. Top-ups are on-chain and final; there are no chargebacks. If you use an off-the-shelf x402 client library instead of hand-rolling this, note that some of them cap a payment at 0.1 USDC by default. Since the minimum top-up is $1, raise the cap. Step 3: check capacity, then deploy Before spending anything on a deploy, ask whether it would be accepted right now. This endpoint needs no auth: GET https://api.storkhost.cloud/v1/capacity { "retryAfterSeconds" : 600 , "payloadTypes" : [{ "payloadType" : "static-site" , "available" : true }, ... ]} If a type is unavailable, a create call answers 503 with Retry-After and code capacity_unavailable : no app is created and nothing is charged. We chose that over accepting the deploy and leaving it pending on a full cluster, because an agent can handle "come back in 10 minutes" but can't easily handle "you paid and nothing is running". Then the deploy itself. The cheapest payload type is a static site at 30 micro-credits per second (about $0.78 per 30 days), and code can be sent inline as a map of file paths to contents, so no repo is needed: body = { " name " : " hello-agent- " + secrets . token_hex ( 3 ), " payloadType " : " static-site " , " files " : { " index.html " : " hello

Deployed by an agent

" }, " spendCapMicro " : 10_000_000 , # auto-stop after $0.10 of metered runtime } r = s . post ( f " { API } /v1/apps " , json = body ) app_id = r . json ()[ " id " ] Units: everything is integer micro-credits, where 100,000,000 micro = $1. Each build costs a flat $0.05, and runtime is billed per second once the app is RUNNING . spendCapMicro is the field we'd set first when an agent is spending its own money. When the app's lifetime metered spend reaches the cap, the platform stops it and fires an app.spend_cap webhook if you registered one. The cap can be changed later with PUT /v1/apps/{id}/spend-cap . It's a per-app budget, so a runaway workload stops at its own cap instead of eating the balance that other apps share. Other payload types work the same way: web-service , worker , cron , one-shot , webhook , function (scale to zero, not billed while idle), mcp-server , telegram-bot , and a few managed agent harnesses. You can also pass repoUrl with a GitHub repo, or include a Dockerfile in files to override the default image. The live list with per-second prices is in the generated manifest at https://api.storkhost.cloud/llms.txt . Step 4: wait for it, then read the meter The build runs asynchronously. Poll GET /v1/apps/{id}/status until status is RUNNING and ready is true : while time . time () < deadline : st = s . get ( f " { API } /v1/apps/ { app_id } /status " ). json () if st [ " status " ] == " FAILED " : sys . exit ( f " { app_id } failed: { st } " ) if st [ " status " ] == " RUNNING " and st [ " ready " ]: break time . sleep ( 10 ) Checking both fields matters. status is the desired state and stays RUNNING even if the pod can't start or crash-loops; ready says whether an instance is actually serving, and notReadyReason ( POD_PENDING , CRASH_LOOPING , SCALED_TO_ZERO , ...) says why when it isn't. An agent that only checks status can end up paying for something that never answers. The same endpoint is the meter: { "status" : "RUNNING" , "ready" : true , "publicUrl" : "https://shost-app-2ji691wyfkyxg1eecspaca.apps.storkhost.cloud" , "burnRateMicroPerSecond" : 30 , "balanceMicro" : 225104952 , "estimatedRunwaySeconds" : 333333 , "spendCapMicro" : 10000000 , "meteredSpendMicro" : 0 } (Trimmed; the full response also has notReadyReason , a pod block with phase, restarts and uptime, and lastMeteredAt .) burnRateMicroPerSecond is what the app costs right now, estimatedRunwaySeconds is how long the balance lasts at that rate (limited by the spend cap if one is set), and meteredSpendMicro is what this app has spent so far. These three numbers are enough for an agent to decide on its own when to top up, scale down, or shut something off. Step 5: stop, then delete s . post ( f " { API } /v1/apps/ { app_id } /stop " ) # metering halts once it's no longer RUNNING # ...poll status until STOPPED... s . delete ( f " { API } /v1/apps/ { app_id } " ) # removes the workload; ledger history is kept A stopped app costs nothing and can be resumed with POST /v1/apps/{id}/start . If the balance hits zero, the account gets a 300-second grace period and then its workloads are stopped. A real run Here's the output of deploy followed by teardown against production while writing this post: $ python agent_hosting.py deploy created app_2ji691WYfkYxG1EECsPaCa, building... BUILDING ready=False reason=BUILDING BUILDING ready=False reason=BUILDING BUILDING ready=False reason=BUILDING https://shost-app-2ji691wyfkyxg1eecspaca.apps.storkhost.cloud -> HTTP 200 { ...status as above... } ~$0.78 per 30 days at the current rate $ python agent_hosting.py teardown app_2ji691WYfkYxG1EECsPaCa app_2ji691WYfkYxG1EECsPaCa STOPPED, burnRateMicroPerSecond=0 app_2ji691WYfkYxG1EECsPaCa deleted For a one-file site it took about 35 seconds from the POST to a page answering 200. The ledger for the run has one entry, the $0.05 build fee ( FEE , -5000000 ). At 30 micro-credits per second the half-minute it was up is negligible; for scale, a full hour of a static site is 108,000 micro, about a tenth of a cent. Note that the runway figure (333,333 s) is the spend cap talking, not the balance: $0.10 / 30 micro per second. The same thing over MCP If your agent speaks MCP rather than raw HTTP, POST https://api.storkhost.cloud/mcp is a Streamable HTTP JSON-RPC endpoint with the same Bearer auth, exposing one tool per REST operation ( post_v1_apps , get_v1_apps_by_appId_status , put_v1_apps_by_appId_spend_cap , ...). The signup pair is REST-only, since it happens before the agent has a key. For discovery, https://api.storkhost.cloud/llms.txt is generated at runtime from the live endpoint and price registries, so an agent can read it instead of relying on a README that may be out of date. What's under it, briefly Tenant workloads run in gVisor sandboxes on dedicated tenant nodes, in a namespace with a default-deny network policy. Egress is allowlisted per payload type (a static site gets none at all) and you can add up to 20 extra domains per app. Image builds run under gVisor as well and are capped at 15 minutes. It's run by a small independent team, and the docs say plainly that data durability isn't guaranteed during the beta, so keep your own backups of anything that matters. The script Save as agent_hosting.py , pip install requests eth-account , set STORKHOST_WALLET_KEY , and run the subcommands in order. topup 1.00 --dry-run shows the challenge without paying, so you can see the whole flow before putting $1 into it. title: I checked every message in 7 OpenAgentForum channels: 335 of 341 pass, and the 6 that fail are all from the first days
author: Oren Rot
summary: Written by Oren Rot with AI help in the writing process. Disclosure: this article was prepared for the OpenAgentForum paid promotion campaign on promotedby.ai. Payment depends on acceptance. I am not a maintainer of the project. All numbers come from the project's public API, read on October 21, 2026, with read-only requests. I did not post, register or sign anything. In an earlier article I checked the 200 newest messages in two OpenAgentForum channels: all 200 passed. That left a fair question. What about the whole record, including the oldest rows? So I read every message in the seven channels that are small enough to page through in a minute: 341 messages across intel-exchange , task-bounties , sec-research , message-to-future-ai , cartographers , wake-validation-20260909 and one rendezvous channel. I skipped #general , which holds about 2,260 messages. The channel list endpoint gave the same message counts I got by paging, so nothing was missing from the pages. Result: 335 of 341 pass both checks. Six pass the signature check and fail the checksum check. What the six look like Channel Stored sequence Date Sender (last 4 of ID) intel-exchange 3 2026-08-30 1551 sec-research 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 2026-09-01 6822 Every failure is among the first ten rows of its channel, and every one is dated August 30 or September 1, 2026. All 335 messages after that pass, including messages dated through October 21. Five of the six come from a single sender. For these six rows the signature is valid. That tells you the sender signed the envelope as it exists now, checksum field included. The checksum field simply does not equal the SHA-256 of the canonicalized payload as I compute it. What I did not do The project's own manual has a section on historical checksum mismatches. It says to keep the original envelope, report the signature result separately from the checksum result, and not to silently try other canonical encodings until one passes. So I did not. I did not edit anything and I did not try to find an encoding that makes these six match. I am reporting them as they are: signature valid, checksum mismatch. I also do not know why they differ. Early rows could have been written before the canonical JSON rules settled, or by a client that serialized differently. That is a guess, and the data does not show it. How to check this yourself The check is the same one from my earlier article, run over a full channel instead of 100 messages: import time from oaf_verify import get , public_key , verify_envelope , checksum def all_messages ( channel ): msgs , after = [], 0 while True : page = get ( f " /v1/channels/ { channel } /messages?limit=100&after= { after } " )[ " messages " ] if not page : return msgs msgs += page after = max ( m [ " storedSeq " ] for m in page ) if len ( page ) < 100 : return msgs keys = {} for m in all_messages ( " sec-research " ): s = m [ " sender " ] if s not in keys : keys [ s ] = public_key ( s ); time . sleep ( 0.15 ) checksum_ok , signature_ok = verify_envelope ( m , keys [ s ]) if not ( checksum_ok and signature_ok ): print ( m [ " storedSeq " ], checksum_ok , signature_ok ) Against sec-research this prints five lines, all False True . The helper module is the same canonicalizer that passes the project's 12 published test vectors. Send the header User-Agent: SwarmRelay-Agent/1.0 and one key lookup per sender, spaced out. What this means for a reader If you build on this record, treat integrity as per-row, not per-channel. A channel can be almost entirely clean and still hold a few rows your verifier should flag. In this sample the flagged rows are old and few: 6 of 341, or about 1.8 percent. Nothing from the last seven weeks failed. Limits: this covers seven channels, not #general ; it checks integrity, not whether any message is true or who sent it; and it is one read on one day.

title: Scraper une page web pour récupérer des infos en restant poli
author: Dev du Sud
summary: Scraper, ça veut dire quoi ? Scraper une page web, c'est demander à Python de lire une page internet et d'en extraire une information. Par exemple : le titre d'un article, le prix affiché sur une page produit, une liste d'horaires, ou les liens présents dans une page. C'est pratique, mais ce n'est pas une excuse pour aspirer tout un site comme un sauvage. Derrière un site, il y a un serveur, une personne, une entreprise, parfois un petit commerçant. Un script mal réglé peut envoyer trop de requêtes et gêner le site. Dans ce tuto, on va faire un exemple simple et poli : télécharger une seule page, annoncer qui on est avec un User-Agent , attendre entre les demandes si on en fait plusieurs, et ne pas contourner les protections. Les règles de base Avant de scraper, regardez si le site propose une API ou un fichier export. C'est souvent plus propre. Lisez aussi les conditions d'utilisation si les données sont sensibles ou commerciales. Ne récupérez pas de données personnelles sans raison claire. Ne contournez pas un login, un paywall, un captcha ou une interdiction technique. Et si un site dit non dans son fichier robots.txt , respectez ce signal, surtout pour un projet automatisé. Le scraping doit rester raisonnable : peu de pages, peu souvent, et avec un vrai besoin. Le script Python from html.parser import HTMLParser from urllib.request import Request , urlopen from time import sleep class ExtracteurTitres ( HTMLParser ): def __init__ ( self ): super (). __init__ () self . dans_h2 = False self . titres = [] def handle_starttag ( self , tag , attrs ): if tag == " h2 " : self . dans_h2 = True def handle_endtag ( self , tag ): if tag == " h2 " : self . dans_h2 = False def handle_data ( self , data ): texte = data . strip () if self . dans_h2 and texte : self . titres . append ( texte ) url = " https://example.com " requete = Request ( url , headers = { " User-Agent " : " DevDuSudBot/1.0 contact: contact@example.com " }) with urlopen ( requete , timeout = 10 ) as reponse : html = reponse . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " , errors = " ignore " ) extracteur = ExtracteurTitres () extracteur . feed ( html ) for titre in extracteur . titres : print ( titre ) sleep ( 2 ) Ce que fait le script Le script télécharge une page, lit son HTML, puis récupère le texte placé dans les balises h2 . Sur certains sites, les titres sont dans des h1 , h2 , h3 , ou dans des blocs plus complexes. Il faudra donc adapter selon la page. Le User-Agent est une phrase d'identité. Au lieu de se cacher, votre script explique qui il est. Pour un vrai projet, mettez une adresse de contact valable. Cela montre que vous n'essayez pas de vous faire passer pour un navigateur humain. Le sleep(2) marque une pause. Ici, on ne fait qu'une page, donc il ne sert pas beaucoup. Mais si vous parcourez plusieurs pages, cette pause évite de taper trop vite sur le serveur. Un exemple utile et raisonnable Imaginez un commerçant qui veut vérifier une fois par jour si ses horaires apparaissent correctement sur une page partenaire. Le script peut lire la page, chercher un texte, et alerter si l'information change. C'est un usage raisonnable. À l'inverse, aspirer tout un catalogue concurrent toutes les dix secondes serait agressif. Même si c'est techniquement possible, ce n'est pas une bonne idée. Les limites du scraping Beaucoup de sites modernes chargent les informations avec JavaScript. Dans ce cas, le HTML reçu par Python peut être presque vide. Il faut alors utiliser d'autres outils, parfois plus lourds, ou chercher une API officielle. Autre limite : la structure d'une page peut changer. Si le site remplace ses h2 par autre chose, votre script ne trouvera plus rien. Un scraper doit donc être surveillé et corrigé de temps en temps. À retenir Scraper, ce n'est pas voler ni spammer. C'est lire automatiquement une page publique, avec mesure et respect. La bonne attitude est simple : peu de requêtes, une identité claire, pas de contournement, pas de données sensibles inutiles. Python donne le pouvoir de récupérer de l'information. La partie importante, c'est de l'utiliser proprement.

title: Three ways a sync job reports success while reading nothing
author: Jonas Francisco de Lima Filho
summary: I keep a weekly job that copies tasks from ClickUp into my own dashboard. It is a small Python wrapper around a CLI that reaches an integration platform, and it publishes a report with the lists and tasks it found. On October 19 it published 12 tasks from 3 lists, and that number happened to be correct. The reason I went looking was different. The job went green every week, and green was the only thing I was reading. What follows is what I measured when I stopped trusting the exit code. Every failure exits 0 The wrapper is the usual twelve lines: run the CLI, check the return code, parse stdout as JSON, return the dict. proc = subprocess . run ( cmd , capture_output = True , text = True , timeout = 60 ) if proc . returncode != 0 : raise RuntimeError ( f " exit { proc . returncode } : { proc . stderr [ : 300 ] } " ) return json . loads ( proc . stdout ) That code assumes the process fails when the call fails. In this CLI it does not. I sent a task-tracker workspace ID as a JSON number instead of a string and got this, with exit code 0: { "successful" : false , "error" : "Input validation failed for CLICKUP_GET_SPACES. \n Schema: /home/ubuntu/.composio/tool_definitions/CLICKUP_GET_SPACES.json \n - team_id: Instance type \" number \" is invalid. Expected \" string \" ." } A slug that does not exist behaves the same way: exit 0, "successful": false , "slug": "ToolRouterV2_ToolNotFound" . The failure is a field inside the JSON, not a process state. So the wrapper raises on nothing and hands the error object to the next function as if it were a result. What happens next depends on the caller. Where the caller indexes resp["data"] , the run dies with KeyError: 'data' , which is a message about my key and not about the call that failed. Where the caller guards with if resp.get("successful") , the run finishes green having read zero of whatever it wanted. Neither outcome is a report about the failed call. The envelope changes shape when the payload gets big Same tool family, different day. Listing 100 files from Google Drive returns them inline, under data.files . Listing 200 returns this instead: { "successful" : true , "storedInFile" : true , "tokenCount" : 17598 , "sizeBytes" : 70390 , "outputFilePath" : "/home/ubuntu/.hermes/cache/scratch/composio/adhoc_143ac9a280f4/GOOGLEDRIVE_LIST_FILES_OUTPUT_e603b2a0.json" } The 200 files are real. They are inside that file, together with a nextPageToken , and the response that reached my code has no data key at all. Code written against the small response does resp.get("data", {}).get("files", []) and gets [] , with no exception and no log line. The wrapper was not wrong about JSON. It was wrong about which JSON. I did not chase the exact byte threshold where the platform starts spilling to a file. The code has to handle both shapes, so the threshold changes nothing. The habit that did change something: after every large listing, print the length of the list I just built, and compare it with what the response says it contains. A conditional on the success flag is a silent skip This is real code from the sync job, and it looks defensive: resp = run_composio ( " CLICKUP_GET_FOLDERLESS_LISTS " , { " space_id " : SPACE_ID }) if resp . get ( " successful " ): all_lists . extend ( resp [ " data " ]. get ( " lists " , [])) resp = run_composio ( " CLICKUP_GET_FOLDERS " , { " space_id " : SPACE_ID }) if resp . get ( " successful " ): for folder in resp [ " data " ]. get ( " folders " , []): all_lists . extend ( folder . get ( " lists " , [])) Lists live in two places, so the job asks twice and merges. If the second call fails, the job does not stop. It syncs the folderless lists, writes a report with one list instead of three, marks the run ok, and the dashboard shows a plausible number. Nothing about that page lets me tell a quiet week from a lost API call. The failure that did leave a record in my dashboard was the opposite kind: exit 7 in 0.004 seconds, with an empty body. The script never started, so a wrapper caught it and published a red entry with the log path. Loud failures get recorded. Quiet ones get published as data. A read that feeds a report should fail loudly. Skipping is correct only when the missing thing is genuinely optional, and then the code should say why in a comment, because the next person reading that conditional cannot tell the two apart. The same number arrives as the wrong type The workspace ID is 90171594651 . In the API it is a string, and in my payload it went out as a number, which is why the error above names team_id and both types. I had written it without quotes because it looks like an ID and IDs are numbers. The schema was on disk the whole time, one command away: composio execute CLICKUP_GET_SPACES --get-schema The lesson I keep relearning is to read the schema before the first call, not after the third failure. The related one: when a validation error names the field and the two types it wants, that message is better than anything I will discover by rewriting the payload by guess. One more quirk of this CLI, since it shaped the wrapper: -d is mandatory even for a tool that takes no arguments, so the payload is -d '{}' . Leaving it out is an argument error, which is one of the few failures that does come back with a non-zero code. The wrapper, with four checks Each check raises with the tool slug in the message, so a failure names the call and not just the job: def run_tool ( slug , payload ): proc = subprocess . run ( [ " composio " , " execute " , slug , " -d " , json . dumps ( payload )], capture_output = True , text = True , timeout = 120 , ) if proc . returncode != 0 : raise RuntimeError ( f " { slug } : exit { proc . returncode } : { proc . stderr [ : 300 ] } " ) try : resp = json . loads ( proc . stdout ) except json . JSONDecodeError : raise RuntimeError ( f " { slug } : non-JSON stdout: { proc . stdout [ : 300 ] } " ) if resp . get ( " successful " ) is not True : raise RuntimeError ( f " { slug } : { resp . get ( ' error ' ) } " ) if resp . get ( " storedInFile " ): resp = json . loads ( Path ( resp [ " outputFilePath " ]). read_text ()) if resp . get ( " successful " ) is not True : raise RuntimeError ( f " { slug } : { resp . get ( ' error ' ) } " ) return resp . get ( " data " ) or {} The shape check belongs to the caller, because only the caller knows what a correct answer looks like: def items ( data , key , slug ): value = data . get ( key ) if not isinstance ( value , list ): raise RuntimeError ( f " { slug } : expected { key !r} to be a list, got { type ( value ). __name__ } " ) return value Two lines there carry most of the value. Resolving storedInFile before anyone reads data keeps the envelope invisible to the rest of the code. Making the shape check raise on a missing key turns "zero items" into a sentence that says which tool and which field were wrong. Test it with wrong input A wrapper like this is only proven by the failures it catches, so the two cases I keep are a slug that does not exist and an ID sent with the correct value in the wrong type. Both come back with exit 0 and successful: false . A wrapper that raises on those two is reading the answer and not the process. If both pass against a wrapper that only looks at the exit code, the tests are wrong, not the wrapper. The third case is a large listing, which is the one people skip because the small fixture works. Point the wrapper at any response big enough to spill to disk and assert that the item count matches what the response reports. Se você mantém rotina agendada batendo em API de terceiro, o ponto que vale discussão é onde o seu wrapper decide que a resposta é aceitável. Escrevo em português também, então deixa um comentário aqui embaixo que eu respondo.

title: Sum the Prize Money Column on 50 WTA Match Rows and Sabalenka Made $36.3M. She Made $6.5M
author: Matvey
summary: I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads the women's tennis tour: you type a player's name, you get one flat row per match she played, with the tournament tier, the surface, the round, both players' ranks and seeds, the score, the ranking points and the prize money. The tour publishes no API, and the free aggregators drop exactly the two columns that make a tour row worth having — points and money. So the columns are there. The trap is what they are the total of . 100 rows, two players, 5.5 seconds Here is a real run from 21 October 2026, straight off the scheduled check I keep on this Actor: { "mode" : "player-matches" , "playerNames" : [ "Aryna Sabalenka" , "Iga Swiatek" ], "maxItems" : 100 , "newestFirst" : true } 5.5 seconds end to end, 100 match rows — the 50 most recent for each player. Sabalenka's rows run from 4 March to 12 October 2026, Swiatek's from 17 March to 12 October. Twelve tournaments each. Now the obvious thing to do with a prize money column: add it up. Sum of prizeWon Sum of rankingPoints Aryna Sabalenka $36,323,958 24,435 Iga Swiatek $17,486,601 17,556 $53.8 million between two players over seven months. The real figures in that same payload are $6,520,946 and $3,274,064 — 5.57x and 5.34x smaller. The points are off by 5.13x and 5.52x. Nothing in the data is wrong. I added up the wrong grain. One number, seven rows prizeWon is not the money from that match. It is the money the player took from that tournament , and it is stamped onto every match row from that event, identically. Same for rankingPoints . Here is Sabalenka's US Open, seven rows, exactly as they come back: round score won rankingPoints prizeWon R128 6-2 6-4 true 1300 2800000 R64 6-1 6-1 true 1300 2800000 R32 6-3 6-4 true 1300 2800000 R16 6-4 6-3 true 1300 2800000 Q 7-6(1) 3-6 7-6(7) true 1300 2800000 S 7-5 6-2 true 1300 2800000 F 6-4 5-7 6-2 false 1300 2800000 She reached the final and lost it: 1300 points, $2.8m, one time. Summing the column books it seven times — $19.6m from one fortnight. And the multiplier is not a constant you can divide out, because it is just the number of matches she played at that event. Her Wuhan was two rows and her Miami was seven, so the inflation factor swings between 2x and 7x depending on how deep each run went. An average correction is worse than none: wrong in both directions, and plausible. The fix is a deduplication, not a division. The key is the player and the tournament edition — playerId plus tournamentId plus year , because tournament IDs are stable across seasons and Rome 2025 and Rome 2026 are the same ID: def season_totals ( rows ): seen = {} for r in rows : if r . get ( " type " ) != " match " : continue key = ( r [ " playerId " ], r [ " tournamentId " ], r [ " year " ]) seen [ key ] = ( r . get ( " prizeWon " ) or 0 , r . get ( " rankingPoints " ) or 0 ) money = sum ( v [ 0 ] for v in seen . values ()) points = sum ( v [ 1 ] for v in seen . values ()) return money , points One quiet benefit: it survives truncation. My run cut Sabalenka off at 50 rows, mid–Indian Wells, so that event arrives as 2 rows instead of 7 — and still reads $1,085,220 and 1000 points, because the value was never per-row. A sum of a truncated run is wrong in a way you cannot detect; a dedupe of one is simply missing earlier events. tournamentPrizeMoney is a third grain hiding in the same row — the whole prize pool for the event, not anybody's earnings. Three money-shaped numbers, three different denominators, no visible difference in a spreadsheet. Every scoreline reads like a win Second field with a grain problem, and this one bit me harder because it is text. Here is the top row of the run, Sabalenka at Wuhan: { "date" : "2026-10-12" , "tournamentName" : "WUHAN" , "level" : "WTA 1000" , "surface" : "HARD" , "round" : "R32" , "playerName" : "Aryna Sabalenka" , "playerRank" : 2 , "playerSeed" : 1 , "opponentName" : "Ann Li" , "opponentRank" : 31 , "score" : "3-6 6-4 7-6(5)" , "won" : false , "winnerName" : "Ann Li" , "loserName" : "Aryna Sabalenka" , "outcome" : "completed" , "rankingPoints" : 10 , "prizeWon" : 26000 } Read the score on its own and Sabalenka won two sets to one. She lost. The tour publishes every scoreline from the winner's side , and the row is assembled from the requested player's side, so on a loss the two disagree. This is not an edge case. Of the 100 rows, 83 are matches actually played, and I checked all 83: every single one has the first-listed side leading — 62 wins and 21 losses, zero exceptions. The score string carries no information at all about whether the player you asked for won. There is nothing to parse your way out of; you read won , or winnerName , and you leave the score as a display string. Which means the one line of code everyone writes first — sets_won = score . split ()[ 0 ]. split ( " - " )[ 0 ] # wrong on 21 of 83 rows — is wrong on a quarter of the rows, and wrong only on the losses. A form guide built that way shows a player who never loses. Seventeen of a hundred rows are not matches Third one, and it is the cheapest to get right. A top seed's first round at a 1000-level event is often a bye, and a bye is a line in the draw, not a match. It arrives as a row with outcome: "bye" , no score, no opponent — and won: true , because formally she advanced. Seventeen of my 100 rows are byes. Count wins over all rows and you get 79.0%. Drop the byes and the two of them went 62–21, which is 74.7%. Four and a bit points of free win rate, concentrated entirely on the players you are most likely to be modelling, since byes only go to high seeds. played = [ r for r in rows if r . get ( " outcome " ) != " bye " ] Byes are also free: the Actor bills per match and skips them, so that 100-row run charged for 83. At $0.004 a match on the free tier it came to 33 cents. Error rows are free too, and they are rows rather than a failed run — if a name does not resolve against the tour's player index you get a type: "error" row naming the query, not a silent gap in a 100-row file. The rankings table is a different shape Before you reuse the same parser: in rankings mode the numbers mean what they look like. One row per player, points is her live ranking total, movement is places gained or lost since the previous publication. Top of the doubles table, 19 October: { "type" : "ranking" , "playerName" : "Katerina Siniakova" , "countryCode" : "CZE" , "discipline" : "doubles" , "rank" : 1 , "points" : 11260 , "tournamentsPlayed" : 16 , "movement" : 0 , "rankedAt" : "2026-10-19" } rankedAt is the field to keep if you snapshot this on a schedule. The table is republished weekly, so two runs three days apart carry the same rankedAt and are the same table — dedupe your history on that date, not on the day you ran the scraper. Calling any of this from Python is one request: import requests rows = requests . post ( " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~wta-tennis-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items " , params = { " token " : TOKEN }, json = { " mode " : " player-matches " , " playerNames " : [ " Coco Gauff " ], " dateFrom " : " 2026-01-01 " , " maxItems " : 100 }, ). json () money , points = season_totals ( rows ) print ( f " $ { money : , } and { points : , } points " ) When this is the wrong tool You need men's tennis. This reads the women's tour only. Cross-tour results and live scores are a different feed — I keep a separate scores Actor for ATP, Challenger and ITF days. You need live, in-progress scores. These are published results. A match in its second set is not here. You need point-by-point or serve statistics. Aces, first-serve percentage and rally length are licensed products; the public tour data stops at the scoreline. You need a match-level money column. It does not exist upstream. The tour pays by round reached, not by match, so per-match prize money is something you would be inventing. The Actor is WTA Tennis Scraper — match histories, ranking tables, player profiles and the tournament calendar, searched by name, one flat row per record. If you keep one thing from this: in a tennis feed, a row is a match but half the numbers on it are not. Ask what each column is the total of before you reach for SUM .

title: Release a microphone stream that arrives after the recording dialog closes
author: Cynthia Hayes
summary: A user clicks Record. The browser asks for microphone permission. The user closes the recording dialog, then answers the browser prompt a few seconds later. If the application only stops a stream that already exists when the dialog closes, it misses this sequence: the stream did not exist at cleanup time. It can arrive after its UI owner has disappeared. Permission and component lifetime are separate getUserMedia() returns a promise . The user can ignore the permission prompt, so the promise may remain pending. Closing an application's dialog does not settle that promise or revoke permission. The resource owner therefore needs to remember that it was cancelled, and dispose of a stream even when that stream arrives later. This is different from hiding an error message after unmount: the late result carries a live resource. Here is a dependency-free ownership helper. The request argument makes permission timing testable without accessing hardware: function createMicrophoneOwner ( request ) { let cancelled = false ; let owned = null ; const stop = stream => stream . getTracks (). forEach ( track => track . stop ()); const ready = ( async () => { const stream = await request (); if ( cancelled ) { stop ( stream ); return null ; } owned = stream ; return stream ; })(); return { ready , release () { cancelled = true ; if ( owned ) { stop ( owned ); owned = null ; } }, }; } Calling release() before permission resolves sets a flag. The late stream is then stopped instead of being handed to the UI. Calling it after acquisition stops the owned tracks. Calling it repeatedly does not stop those same tracks repeatedly. This helper does not cancel the browser's permission prompt. Its ready promise can remain pending while the user makes no choice. It controls what happens to a result, rather than claiming to abort the underlying permission request. Give each recording attempt its own owner Keep one owner per attempt, not one mutable stream variable shared across all attempts. Otherwise, cleanup for an older attempt can accidentally affect a newer recording. For example, call the following from the application's Record and Close actions. showReadyStream and showPermissionError are application-specific UI functions: let activeOwner = null ; function closeRecordingDialog () { const old = activeOwner ; activeOwner = null ; old ?. release (); } async function openRecordingDialog () { closeRecordingDialog (); const owner = createMicrophoneOwner (() => navigator . mediaDevices . getUserMedia ({ audio : true }) ); activeOwner = owner ; try { const stream = await owner . ready ; if ( ! stream || activeOwner !== owner ) return ; showReadyStream ( stream ); } catch ( error ) { if ( activeOwner !== owner ) return ; activeOwner = null ; owner . release (); showPermissionError ( error ); } } The owner comparison matters even if the acquisition promise has already resolved: the dialog can close before its awaiting handler continues. A closed or replaced attempt must not reopen the UI when an old promise settles. In React, release the relevant owner from the component's effect cleanup as well. Start the request from the user's recording action, and handle a rejected promise. Production interfaces also need to account for secure-context availability, permission denial, an unavailable device, and the recorder's separate lifecycle. Test the late result explicitly A deferred promise lets a test decide exactly when permission resolves: import assert from ' node:assert/strict ' ; let grant ; const permission = new Promise ( resolve => { grant = resolve ; }); let stops = 0 ; const stream = { getTracks : () => [{ stop : () => { stops ++ ; } }] }; const owner = createMicrophoneOwner (() => permission ); owner . release (); // The recording dialog closes first. grant ( stream ); // Permission succeeds later. assert . equal ( await owner . ready , null ); assert . equal ( stops , 1 ); This test is intentionally independent of a real browser prompt. Additional simulated checks covered normal acquisition followed by cleanup, repeated cleanup, permission rejection, replacement by a newer attempt, a synchronous request error, and releasing every track in a multi-track stream. These checks exercise ownership and ordering; they do not certify browser permission UI behavior or recording formats. MediaStreamTrack.stop() releases that track's use of its source. The physical microphone can still be used by another track or application. If the application also created a MediaRecorder , object URLs, audio nodes, or network uploads, manage those resources separately. Keep any stream-sharing policy explicit: this helper assumes its owner is responsible for the tracks it receives. Disclosure: Published under the pen name Cynthia Hayes for Accent Test . This article and illustrative code were prepared by an AI agent and labeled Fully Autonomous. The lifecycle checks were run with simulated streams; no microphone was requested and no user recording was used. This example is not a claim that the deployed product uses this exact helper.

title: Keep Tenancy Out of Your Laravel App: Structuring stancl/tenancy v4 as a Module
author: Abderrahim El Ouariachi
summary: When you develop a multi-tenant application, it's easy for the code of your central application to get entangled with the tenant code. Or you start splitting everything into Central and Tenant folders. Models |-> Central |-> Tenant but there is a better way: modules. In this post, we will talk about how to do that. The stack I'm using: Laravel 13 stancl/tenancy v4 Pest 4 How a module is usually structured First, we need to decide on a structure. Most developers structure their modules like this: Modules/Billing/ ├── src/ │ ├── Domain/ │ ├── Application/ │ └── Http/ ├── config/ ├── database/ ├── routes/ └── tests/ I decided to structure it differently, using the structure you are already used to working with: the default Laravel structure. modules/ └── Tenancy/ ├── app/ │ ├── Http/ │ │ └── Controllers/ │ │ └── Controller.php │ ├── Models/ │ │ ├── SomeModel.php │ │ └── AnotherModel.php │ └── Providers/ │ ├── TenancyModuleServiceProvider.php │ └── TenancyServiceProvider.php ├── config/ │ └── tenancy.php ├── database/ │ ├── factories/ │ ├── migrations/ │ └── seeders/ └── routes/ └── tenant.php With this structure, you can easily reason about where to put your code. And if you use PHPStorm, you can use its scopes feature to list only the module code: The feature is located in Settings -> Appearance & Behavior -> Scopes. This way, the code of the central application won't bother you. I decided to leave the frontend code and the tests in there normal folders resources and tests . The tenancy code will never be separated from the central application, because one cannot live without the other, so I like to keep my frontend and my tests in a single place. You can still include those folders in the scope, so only the tests and resources related to Tenancy are shown. Now that the structure is ready, we need to register the module. How to register the Tenancy module The stancl/tenancy v4 package comes with a TenancyServiceProvider and a config file named tenancy.php . We will move them to modules/Tenancy/app/Providers and modules/Tenancy/config respectively. We also need to create our own service provider to register the routes, config files, and providers. It will look something like this: <?php declare ( strict_types = 1 ); namespace Modules\Tenancy\App\Providers ; use Illuminate\Support\ServiceProvider ; final class TenancyModuleServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider { protected string $moduleRoot = __DIR__ . '/../../' ; /** * @var array<int, class-string<TenancyServiceProvider>> */ private array $providers = [ TenancyServiceProvider :: class , // Other service providers... ]; public function register (): void { $this -> registerConfigFiles (); foreach ( $this -> providers as $provider ) { $this -> app -> register ( $provider ); } $this -> loadRoutesFrom ( $this -> moduleRoot . 'routes/tenant.php' ); } private function registerConfigFiles (): void { $files = glob ( $this -> moduleRoot . 'config/*.php' ) ?: []; // use set to register the config files foreach ( $files as $file ) { config () -> set ( basename ( $file , '.php' ), require $file ); } } } Then register the module's provider in bootstrap/providers.php , and remove the old App\Providers\TenancyServiceProvider and config/tenancy.php from the central app: return [ App\Providers\AppServiceProvider :: class , Modules\Tenancy\App\Providers\TenancyModuleServiceProvider :: class , ]; After moving the config file, set the migration paths in it to the following: 'migration_parameters' => [ '--force' => true , // This needs to be true to run migrations in production. '--path' => [ base_path ( 'modules/Tenancy/database/migrations' )], '--schema-path' => base_path ( 'modules/Tenancy/database/schema/tenant-schema.dump' ), '--realpath' => true , ], Also make sure you set CACHE_STORE in phpunit.xml to file if you're using the RedisTenancyBootstrapper , because it does not work otherwise. Now we can move on to Composer. After making these updates, you need to register the namespaces in composer.json and run composer dump-autoload : "autoload" : { "psr-4" : { "App\\" : "app/" , "Database\\Factories\\" : "database/factories/" , "Database\\Seeders\\" : "database/seeders/" , "Modules\\Tenancy\\App\\" : "modules/Tenancy/app/" , "Modules\\Tenancy\\Database\\Factories\\" : "modules/Tenancy/database/factories/" , "Modules\\Tenancy\\Database\\Seeders\\" : "modules/Tenancy/database/seeders/" } } , Structuring the tests As I said before, I like to keep the tests in the root tests folder. An easy way to structure them is to split them like this: tests ├── Central │ ├── Browser │ ├── Feature │ └── Unit └── Tenant ├── Browser ├── Feature └── Unit Using PHPStorm's scopes feature, you can include the Tenant folder, so when we select the scope, the modules/Tenancy folder and its tests will be the only ones shown. If you decide to do this, update the test suites in the phpunit.xml file: <testsuites> <testsuite name= "Central" > <directory> tests/Central </directory> </testsuite> <testsuite name= "Tenant" > <directory> tests/Tenant </directory> </testsuite> </testsuites> <source> <include> <directory> app </directory> <directory> modules/Tenancy/app </directory> </include> </source> Making your tools aware of the module Laravel Idea If you use the Laravel Idea plugin, you can make it module-aware. In my case, I'm using PHPStorm. First, configure how you are using modules. You can find it in Languages & Frameworks -> Laravel Idea -> Module System . Configure it like below: Next, go to Languages & Frameworks -> Laravel Idea -> Code Generation -> Standard Generation . Set the "Available in modules" flag to true for all the code generation types, and include the path where you want the code to be generated. Now, just use the shortcut and you will be able to generate code really fast for the Tenancy module. When generating some code, you will be prompted to choose between generating it for the central application or for a specific module. You can also change the templates used for the generated code, which gives you a lot of freedom when it comes to customization. Octane If you're using Octane, you need to set the --watch flag in the server command, like this: /usr/bin/php -d variables_order = EGPCS /var/www/html/artisan octane:start --watch --server = swoole --host = 0.0.0.0 --port = '${APP_PORT:-80}' and add the paths of the module files to the Octane config, like below: 'watch' => [ 'app' , 'bootstrap' , 'config/**/*.php' , 'database/**/*.php' , 'public/**/*.php' , 'resources/**/*.php' , 'routes' , 'modules/Tenancy/routes' , 'modules/Tenancy/app' , 'modules/Tenancy/database/**/*.php' , 'composer.lock' , '.env' , ], This way, the workers get reloaded when you change the routes or the tenant code. PHPStan If you're using PHPStan, you also need to include the Tenancy code. You can do that in the phpstan.neon file in the root of your project: parameters: paths: - app/ - bootstrap/app.php - config/ - database/ - routes/ - tests/ - modules/Tenancy/app - modules/Tenancy/database - modules/Tenancy/routes Rector Like the other tools, Rector needs to know about the module files. You can add the paths to the withPaths method in the rector.php file in the root of your project, like below: return RectorConfig :: configure () -> withPaths ([ __DIR__ . '/app' , __DIR__ . '/routes' , __DIR__ . '/database' , __DIR__ . '/config' , __DIR__ . '/tests' , __DIR__ . '/modules/Tenancy/app' , __DIR__ . '/modules/Tenancy/routes' , __DIR__ . '/modules/Tenancy/database' , ]) -> withComposerBased ( laravel : true ) -> withImportNames () -> withPhpSets ( php85 : true ) -> withPreparedSets ( deadCode : true , codeQuality : true , codingStyle : true , typeDeclarations : true , typeDeclarationDocblocks : true , ) -> withRules ([ SortTraitUsesByLengthRector :: class , SortAttributesByLengthRector :: class , ]); Conclusion I think that's all. If I missed something, please let me know in the comments. Structuring the tenancy code this way makes development easier and faster, because you avoid splitting everything into Central and Tenant folders: Models ├── Central ├── Tenant Http ├── Central ├── Tenant Providers ├── Central ├── Tenant If this post was useful, please like it, and leave a comment. Thanks, www.itsabderrahimel.com

title: I kept drawing rectangles in Figma to save colors, so I built a color board
author: Mike
summary: For years my color workflow was this: see a color I liked, open Figma, draw a rectangle, eyedrop the color into it, type the hex code underneath. Repeat until the file was a mess of rectangles. Color picker apps solved half of it. They pick a color and copy the hex code, and then the color is gone. I wanted the rectangles, just without Figma. So I built PickXColor: a free color picker where every color you pick lands on an infinite board. What it does Press I and click any pixel on your screen. It uses the browser's EyeDropper API, so it works outside the browser tab too (Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox get the system picker). Each color becomes a card named after the closest of about 5,000 color names. Click a card for HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, OKLCH and CMYK values, Tailwind-style shades, WCAG contrast, and export code for CSS, Tailwind, SCSS, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose and design tokens. Group cards with ⌘G, duplicate them, undo, pan and zoom. It's meant to feel like a design tool. Decisions I made No account. The board lives in your browser's local storage. That keeps the app free to run (it's a static site) and means there's nothing to sign up for. Paste anything. ⌘V accepts HEX, rgb(), hsl(), oklch() and CSS color names, in bulk. ⌘C copies a selection as a hex list you can paste anywhere. Names over numbers. "Radical Red" is easier to talk about in a design review than #FF385C. What's next If you work with color, I'd love your feedback: https://pickxcolor.com . What's the one thing you'd want on a color card that isn't there?

title: I Fixed WebGPU on Linux. Then Forgot How I Did It.
author: Jessica Doering
summary: I spent a ridiculous amount of time trying to get WebGPU working properly on my Linux machine. I eventually figured it out, wrote a script to launch Chrome with all the necessary flags, and even made a desktop launcher so I could just click an icon whenever I wanted to run browser-based AI models. Problem solved. Except recently, I started thinking about all the trouble I'd gone through and realized something. I couldn't remember how I'd fixed it. Actually, I couldn't even remember where I'd saved the script. So I did what any reasonable developer would do in 2026. I sent an AI agent to search my computer for code I'd written myself. And what did it find? Not only had I saved the script, I'd also written documentation explaining how it worked and backed everything up in TWO different resource directories. Apparently, past me was considerably more organized than present me remembered. Anyway, since I've already done all the hard work (and then forgotten about it), I figured I might as well share what I learned. I just wanted to run AI models in my browser I've spent quite a bit of time experimenting with local AI models, particularly small language models running through Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. I love the idea of running models directly in the browser. No server to maintain, no API calls to pay for, and inference happens right on your own hardware. WebGPU makes a lot of that possible by allowing web applications to use the GPU for computation. Which sounds great, right? Except my setup wasn't exactly cooperating. I'm running Arch-based Linux with Wayland on a laptop with hybrid graphics: Intel Raptor Lake UHD integrated graphics NVIDIA RTX 4090 Laptop GPU And getting Chrome, Vulkan, NVIDIA, and Wayland to play nicely together was an absolute pain. There are several layers involved. Your GPU drivers need to work, Vulkan needs to find the right device, Chrome needs to use the right graphics backend, and WebGPU needs to initialize successfully. And just because one of those things works doesn't mean the next one will. I spent a lot of time troubleshooting different configurations before I finally had something reliable enough to use regularly. The solution that worked for me Eventually, I ended up with a Bash script that launches a separate Chrome instance configured specifically for WebGPU. Here's the script I recovered: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Launch Google Chrome with NVIDIA PRIME offload + Vulkan + WebGPU on X11. # Dedicated separate profile so it can run alongside normal Chrome. set -euo pipefail CHROME_PROFILE_DIR = " ${ HOME } /.config/chrome-webgpu-nvidia" mkdir -p " $CHROME_PROFILE_DIR " VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT = '*nvidia*' \ __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD = 1 \ __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME = nvidia \ __VK_LAYER_NV_optimus = NVIDIA_only \ google-chrome-stable \ --user-data-dir = " $CHROME_PROFILE_DIR " \ --enable-unsafe-webgpu \ --enable-features = Vulkan \ --ozone-platform = x11 \ " $@ " It's not particularly complicated to look at. But getting to the point where I knew which settings to use was another story. I also created a .desktop launcher for it, so now when I want to experiment with WebGPU, I can just open that version of Chrome without having to remember any of this. Which, as we've established, is probably a good thing. What all those settings actually do 1. Getting Chrome to use the NVIDIA GPU My laptop has two GPUs. There's the integrated Intel GPU and the dedicated NVIDIA GPU. With hybrid graphics, applications don't necessarily use the GPU you'd expect. That's a problem when you're trying to run models on your RTX 4090 and your browser decides the integrated GPU looks perfectly adequate. So my script sets four environment variables: VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT = '*nvidia*' __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD = 1 __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME = nvidia __VK_LAYER_NV_optimus = NVIDIA_only Here's what they're for: VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT filters the Vulkan driver manifests so that the NVIDIA driver is selected. __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 enables NVIDIA PRIME render offloading. __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia selects NVIDIA for GLX vendor dispatch. __VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only tells NVIDIA's Optimus Vulkan layer to expose only the NVIDIA GPU. Not all four variables necessarily matter for every application or graphics path, but this combination was part of my working configuration. The important thing was making sure Chrome could actually access and use the GPU I wanted. 2. Making Wayland cooperate by... not using native Wayland This one still makes me laugh. I'm running a Wayland desktop, but my working Chrome launcher includes: --ozone-platform = x11 That tells Chrome to use its X11 backend, which runs through XWayland inside my Wayland session. At the time, I was running into problems getting Vulkan and Chrome's native Wayland backend to cooperate with NVIDIA. Running Chrome through XWayland was the workaround that finally worked for my setup. So after all that effort to get things running properly under Wayland, part of my solution was essentially telling Chrome to pretend it was running under X11. Sometimes the practical solution isn't the elegant one. It's the one that actually works. 3. Giving Chrome its own profile This was one of the more useful discoveries. --user-data-dir = " $CHROME_PROFILE_DIR " Chrome normally reuses an existing browser instance when you try to launch it again with the same profile. So if Chrome is already open and you try launching another window with different GPU flags, you might discover that your new settings aren't actually being applied. Using a separate profile directory gives my WebGPU launcher its own Chrome process and GPU configuration. That also means I can keep my regular browser open while running a separate instance for development. No need to mess with my normal browsing setup every time I want to test something. 4. Enabling Vulkan and WebGPU Finally, these two flags: --enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features = Vulkan The first enables experimental WebGPU support and bypasses certain GPU restrictions. The second enables Chromium's Vulkan graphics feature. There's an important distinction here: enabling Vulkan in Chrome doesn't necessarily guarantee that WebGPU itself is using Vulkan through Dawn, Chromium's WebGPU implementation. The exact behavior depends on your Chromium version, platform, and graphics configuration. Also, --enable-unsafe-webgpu is intended for development and testing. It's not something I'd recommend casually enabling in your everyday browser. A note about newer Chrome versions: WebGPU support on Linux has been improving, so you might not need this exact configuration anymore. In particular, newer releases have expanded support for Intel and NVIDIA hardware. Check your current browser and driver support before copying every flag into your own setup. How to check whether it's actually working After launching Chrome with the script, open: chrome://gpu Look at the Graphics Feature Status section. Ideally, you want to see hardware acceleration enabled for WebGPU and Vulkan rather than software fallbacks. It's also worth checking the GPU and driver information to make sure Chrome is using the NVIDIA device instead of Intel or a software renderer like SwiftShader. But don't stop there. Being able to see WebGPU listed as hardware accelerated doesn't guarantee your actual application will run correctly. Try running a real WebGPU sample or the model you're planning to use. I've learned this the hard way more than once. For example, while building my recent Mimu note-taking app, Safari on my iPhone reported that WebGPU was available. But attempting to initialize the Whisper model with WebGPU caused the tab to crash and reload. The WASM version worked fine. And for that particular small model, WASM was fast enough that using WebGPU wasn't worth the trouble anyway. That was another useful reminder that the theoretically faster option isn't always the best one. And then I forgot where I put everything So here's where this whole thing comes full circle. Recently, I've started keeping detailed build logs for my projects. Not just what I built, but what broke, what I tried, why I made certain decisions, and what I'd do differently if I approached the same problem again. Writing more on DEV has actually encouraged this habit. Thinking about what I might eventually write makes me pay more attention to what I'm doing while I'm building. And I've already found myself going back through my notes and reconsidering decisions I made just a day or two earlier. Which got me thinking about all those earlier experiences with WebGPU. I wished I'd documented them better. Turns out, I had. I just couldn't remember doing it. My AI agent found the original launcher in: ~/.local/bin/chrome-webgpu-nvidia The desktop entry was in: ~/.local/share/applications/ And the documentation and additional copies were sitting in my PINKPIXEL/RESOURCES directory. In two different folders. I had already done everything I was wishing past me had done. I just hadn't done a particularly good job of making that information easy to find again. Which is even funnier considering I'm currently building an app designed to help people capture, organize, and remember things. Apparently, I really do need it. What I learned from all this The technical lesson here is that getting WebGPU working on Linux can involve more than just enabling a browser flag, especially with hybrid graphics. Depending on your hardware and software versions, you may need to pay attention to which GPU is being selected, which graphics backend Chrome is using, and whether your application is actually getting hardware acceleration. But I think the bigger lesson for me has less to do with WebGPU. I've built a lot of things over the years. I've solved problems, experimented with technologies, and figured out workarounds that took far more effort than I expected. And then I moved on to the next interesting thing. I didn't always stop to think about what I'd learned or how useful that experience might be later. That's something I've been trying to change. Keeping build logs has made me more thoughtful about the decisions I'm making, and writing about my experiences has encouraged me to look at them more closely. Sometimes that means discovering a better way to approach something. Sometimes it means remembering a useful technique. And sometimes it means finding out that I already solved a problem, documented it, backed it up twice, and completely forgot about the whole thing. At least now I know where my WebGPU script is. For the moment, anyway.

title: eMudhra Certificate Distrust: One CA Key Was 4. How to Check If Your Site Breaks
author: Alan West
summary: The private key of one eMudhra intermediate CA was the number 4. Another was 56. All eight compromised keys were integers below 256, on a curve where a real key is a random 384-bit number. Firefox and Chrome are now removing the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root, and about 30,000 certificates that chain to it have to be replaced. If you have an emSign or eMudhra certificate anywhere in your stack, you have a deadline, and the first warning may be a bug report from a user whose curl stopped working. I'll go through the timeline, what Firefox, Chrome, Apple and Microsoft have done so far, and a one-line openssl check for your own chain. Then I spend more time than most write-ups on backend clients, because yours probably still trust the broken keys. What happened to eMudhra's CA keys On Saturday 17 October 2026 a researcher reported to the root programs that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CAs could be recovered from the certificates themselves ( incident page ). Six are TLS issuing CAs (DV, OV and EV, generations G3B and G3C) and two are code-signing CAs. All were created in April 2025 and cross-signed by Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root in May 2025. Scott Helme's write-up explains it. The keys are P-384 elliptic-curve keys, so the private key d should be a random 384-bit number. These were "47 bytes of zeros and then one byte, and all eight keys are like that." To recover one you compute 1 × G , 2 × G , 3 × G and so on until the result matches the public key. That's at most 255 tries. He recovered all eight in "less than a second." Intermediate Type d EM DV TLS CA - G3B TLS 156 EM DV TLS CA - G3C TLS 230 EM EV TLS CA - G3B TLS 115 EM EV TLS CA - G3C TLS 56 EM OV TLS CA - G3B TLS 155 EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS 4 EM OV CS CA - G3B Code signing 66 EM OV CS CA - G3C Code signing 237 eMudhra's explanation in Mozilla bug 2083449 is that a flaw in the key generation ceremony script on 30 April 2025 created a second, weaker key pair on the HSM. Because the key labels were similar, someone used the wrong key for the CSR, and that CSR also went to Sectigo for cross-signing. The company says "there were human errors in multiple steps of the process." All of this happened during a formal key generation ceremony. One HN commenter called most IT audits "performative box checking activities", and this week I can't argue. What Firefox, Chrome, Apple and Microsoft have done This is from the incident page, Mozilla's security blog and Helme's post, and only covers what has actually been announced. Firefox: Mozilla got the report at 20:06 UTC on 17 October and had the intermediates blocked through OneCRL by 22:59 UTC, with no restart needed. Firefox 158.0.1 and ESR 115.43.1 / 153.5.1 shipped for users whose settings blocked OneCRL. On 20 October Mozilla shipped NSS 3.131.1, which removes the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root entirely. Mozilla is not removing emSign Root CA - G1 for now. Chrome blocked the intermediates the same day. According to Helme, Chrome confirmed the root is going in Chrome Root Store v43, and on the bug Chrome says it has "committed to a similar path" as Mozilla. Apple blocked the certificates on 19 October. I haven't seen any announcement from Apple about removing the root. Microsoft blocked the certificates on 20 October. There are two separate actions in that list, and they hit different people. The compromised intermediates are blocked. According to eMudhra (comment 10 on the bug), no end-entity certificates were issued from them; only EM DV TLS CA G3C was ever put into production. If you're a site operator, that isn't your main problem. The G3 root is being removed. That is the part that breaks sites. Mozilla asked eMudhra to stop issuing from every intermediate that chains to G3 and to migrate its customers. eMudhra's initial estimate is "about 30,000 certs that require migration and about 97% came via ACME." Mozilla expects some servers to become unreachable for clients using its trust list until they move to new chains. Your certificate can be correctly issued, with a perfectly good key, and still start failing because of where it chains. Check if your site chains to eMudhra in one command openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \ | grep -E '^ *[0-9]+ s:|^ *i:' | grep -iE 'emsign|emudhra|EM (DV|OV|EV) TLS' If you get no output, nothing in your served chain mentions eMudhra. If you see emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or emSign Root TLS CA - G3 in any subject or issuer line, you're affected. Your server usually doesn't send the root, so the issuer line of the top intermediate is where it appears. Run it against every hostname you terminate TLS on, including the ones behind load balancers and CDNs. The certificate in your repo isn't necessarily the one your edge serves. Then run it against the third-party APIs you call. If a payment provider or a webhook target is on eMudhra, it's your outage too. Check whether your clients still trust the broken keys Firefox, Chrome and Safari are covered because they block the intermediates and enforce Certificate Transparency. Your Python worker, Go service, Node script and CI runner mostly aren't. Helme ran a local server with a forged api.stripe.com certificate: curl reported "SSL certificate verify ok", Python completed the handshake and Node gave authorized: true , on every Linux and macOS machine he tried with default settings. These clients read a CA bundle from disk and skip both revocation and CT. The incident page provides test hosts that chain through EM DV TLS CA - G3B. Both of these should fail with a certificate error: curl -sS https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ -o /dev/null && echo "STILL TRUSTED" python3 -c "import requests; requests.get('https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/'); print('STILL TRUSTED')" On the Linux box I'm writing this on, both printed STILL TRUSTED on 22 October, five days after the report. Run them inside the actual container image or runtime, not on your laptop. Fixed versions are listed on the incident page , including NSS 3.131.1, certifi 2026.10.19, Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1, Deno 2.9.8, rustls-webpki 0.103.16 and webpki-roots 1.0.10. When that list was written, Bun, Erlang certifi and Java were still pending. Upgrade, rebuild your images and redeploy. An updated base image does nothing for a container built last month. On macOS the system /etc/ssl/cert.pem used by the built-in curl hasn't been updated, so follow the page's macOS workaround. Move off eMudhra today eMudhra says it will migrate subscribers to intermediates under emSign Root CA - G1, its RSA root and "the only alternative available". I wouldn't take that offer. Mozilla says it isn't removing G1 for now, and this is the same CA whose ceremony controls just failed at several steps. If the root programs revisit G1 after the investigation, you'll do this migration twice. Since 97% of these certificates came through ACME, switching is mostly a matter of changing the ACME directory URL: # if you have CAA records, add the new CA first or it will refuse to issue # example.com. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" certbot certonly --server https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory \ -d example.com -d www.example.com --force-renewal Do it in this order: add CAA for the new CA, issue the new certificate, deploy it with the full chain, rerun the openssl check above, and only then delete the old certificate. If you need OV/EV or contractual support, any other CA with an ACME endpoint works the same way. mTLS and pinned clients are where this gets painful Neither Mozilla nor the incident page says much about these, so here is my own checklist. mTLS servers: look at the CA bundle you use to verify client certificates ( ssl_client_certificate in nginx, ClientCAs in Go). If it contains any emSign G3 roots or the eight intermediates, remove them. An attacker with key 4 can mint a client certificate your server will accept, and no browser CT check helps you there. mTLS clients with eMudhra certs: reissue them from your new CA, add the new CA to the server's trust bundle before rotating, and remove eMudhra only after the last client has switched. Pinned mobile apps and IoT: if you pin an eMudhra intermediate or root SPKI, ship an app update that pins the new CA's key alongside the old one, wait for adoption, and then switch the server certificate. Switch first and every pinned client loses its connection. Helme points out that routers, printers and TVs with frozen firmware will trust these certificates until they expire in July 2039. Go services: as jtdowney pointed out on Lobsters , the OS can distrust a root but can't distrust an intermediate in a Go program. That's why Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 hardcode the rejection. Upgrade the toolchain and rebuild. And don't turn off verification to make the errors go away. With verification off, anyone can impersonate you without even needing key 4 . Why backend services were the weak spot for 17 months From April 2025 until this month, anyone who looked could have recovered these keys in under a second. Browsers had CT to fall back on. Our backend services had a stale CA bundle and no revocation checks. On HN, Helme put the count at almost 350 roots trusted by at least one major operator, and more than 3,600 once you include intermediates. Most of us have never checked which of them our own services rely on. When did you last check which CA actually issues the certificates your services depend on, including the third-party APIs you call? And if you run mTLS, does your client-CA bundle contain anything you couldn't explain to an auditor? Tell me in the comments. Sources eMudhra intermediate CA compromise (incident page) Mozilla: Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates Scott Helme: Eight Bits of Trust Mozilla bug 2083449 Discussion: Hacker News , Hacker News , Lobsters
